headline: Nasdaq record. Ten-year at a 24-year high.
standfirst: Monday ran three stories at once. In Brazil, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro finished the presidential first round ahead of President Lula, 47.0% to 45.2%, against polls that had Lula leading, and the Ibovespa jumped 7.7% to a record 206,921, its biggest one-day gain since March 2020, as the dollar fell about 4% to R$5.00 and the Brazil ETF rose 12.5%; the runoff is on 25 October. On Wall Street the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.05% to a record 27,477.31 on Nvidia's third straight record, the S&P 500 gained 0.66% to 7,773.95, within 0.3% of its summer high, and the Dow 0.18% to 51,267.90. And bonds sold off: ISM services prices paid rose to 74.0, the highest since July 2022, and the ten-year touched 5.349%, the highest since 2002, before closing near 5.31%, with October's Fed hike still about 20–22% priced. Brent fell about 2% to $100.3 on a G7 stock release and Gulf exports at pre-war levels, though tankers were attacked again and Iran's president called talks meaningless. The euro touched $1.116, its lowest since May 2025, on French and Spanish politics. Asia is higher, the Nikkei near 70,700 and Hong Kong up 0.7%, with Korea down about 1% on its reopening and mainland China shut until 8 October. Today: the BoJ's Ueda, the trade balance, Williams, Musalem, Bowman and Schmid, and the first of three Treasury auctions.

bullets.title: Rates: services growth slowed, services prices hit a four-year high, and the ten-year touched its highest since 2002
bullets.text: The ISM services index fell to 54.9 from 55.4 against 55.0 expected, with business activity down to 56.5 from 61.7, new orders 59.8 and export orders in contraction at 46.9, but the prices index rose to 74.0 from 72.6 against 73.3 expected, its highest since July 2022, and employment rose back above 50 to 50.1. S&P Global's services index was revised to 58.8, the fastest expansion in more than five years. The ten-year touched 5.349% and closed near 5.31%, up about 3bp; the thirty-year touched 5.703% and closed near 5.66%, up about 3bp; the two-year held near 4.84%. The long Treasury ETF fell 0.48% and is down 6.2% over a month. October's Fed hike is priced at about 20–22%, a hold at 76–80%, with a hike by December fully priced in swaps; Jefferies' Thomas Simons says the survey comments cite fuel, shipping and interest costs, and BMO Asset Management's head of bonds says a thirty-year yield above 6% is inevitable this month. A very large crude carrier now costs about $1.6 million a day to charter, 24 times the 2025 rate, according to Clarksons. Supply is the test this week: $58 billion of three-year notes today at 13:00 ET, $39 billion of ten-year notes tomorrow and $22 billion of thirty-year bonds on Thursday, with the minutes of the 16 September meeting tomorrow at 14:00 ET. Japan's ten-year auction drew firmer demand than last month's, with the yield near 3.1%.

bullets.title: Equities: a record Nasdaq led by Nvidia, a small gain in the broad index, and Asia and Europe following
bullets.text: The Nasdaq Composite closed at a record 27,477.31, up 1.05% after touching 27,544 intraday, and the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.87% to a record 31,076; the S&P 500 rose 0.66% to 7,773.95, the Dow 0.18% to 51,267.90 and the Russell 2000 0.50% to 2,847.14, and the VIX closed at 15.52. Nvidia rose 2.1% to a record $238.90, its third straight, with a market value above $5.7 trillion that options traders see crossing $6 trillion by the end of the month; Microsoft gained 1.5%, Meta 1.9% and Tesla 2.2%, SpaceX 7.6% and Micron fell 1.3%. Materials rose 1.31%, communication services 1.17%, energy 1.00% and financials 0.73%, while real estate fell 0.34%; the equal-weight S&P 500 fund is down about 3.6% over a month against a 0.7% gain for the cap-weighted index. Europe was mixed on Monday: the Stoxx 600 rose 0.4%, the DAX 0.1%, the FTSE 100 and Swiss index 0.3% each, while the CAC 40 fell 0.8% on French budget worries; the euro-area composite PMI rose to 53.1, the fastest in about three and a half years. In Asia the Nikkei is up about 1% near 70,700 after Monday's 2.4% jump to 69,947, Hong Kong up 0.7%, Taiwan 0.2% and Australia 0.6%, and Korea is down about 1% on its first session after the holiday; mainland China is shut until 8 October. Earnings season starts quietly: Constellation Brands and Levi Strauss tomorrow, PepsiCo on Thursday, Delta on Friday, the banks on the 13th.

bullets.title: Brazil: a first-round upset, a 7.7% day and the biggest currency move in four years
bullets.text: Sunday's presidential first round put Flavio Bolsonaro at 47.03% of valid votes, 56.1 million, against Lula's 45.16%, 53.9 million, where polls had Lula ahead by about three points; neither cleared 50%, so the runoff is on 25 October. His allies also gained in Congress, which analysts say would make a tighter-spending, privatisation and tax-cut agenda easier to pass if he wins. The Ibovespa closed at a record 206,921, up 7.71% and its largest one-day gain since 24 March 2020; the dollar fell 4.12% to R$5.001, the real's best day since 2022. The Brazil ETF rose 12.5% in New York, Itau Unibanco about 15%, Bradesco 19%, Nu Holdings 14%, Petrobras 12% and MercadoLibre 8%, while B3 rose more than 20% and the pulp exporter Suzano fell as much as 8.5% on the stronger currency. Argentina's ETF rose 5.9%, Chile's 2.4% and Mexico's 1.1%. Brazil's deficit was close to 10% of GDP in June, according to CNBC. In 2022 a better-than-expected first round for the elder Bolsonaro produced a 5.5% equity gain and a currency gain of more than 4% the next day; Societe Generale had forecast R$5.10 by the end of 2026 before Monday's move.

bullets.title: Oil and Iran: a stock release and recovering exports against a shipping war that has not stopped
bullets.text: December Brent settled near $100.3, down about 1.9%, and WTI near $89.4, down 1.8%; this morning Brent is near $100.3–100.7 and WTI $89.3–89.6. The G7 agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel from emergency stocks and avoid export restrictions; the top OPEC+ producers left November production targets unchanged; JPMorgan puts Middle East crude exports at 17.5 million barrels a day, 98% of pre-war, and products at 3 million, 58%. Against that, at least 11 tankers have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz since last Monday, five incidents were reported on Monday alone, a tanker turned back after an IRGC warning, and US Central Command says it has redirected 130 vessels since resuming its blockade of Iranian ports on 14 July and destroyed 13 it says violated it. Iran's president called talks with Washington meaningless; Foreign Minister Araghchi says Qatar will relay a final US response, expected today; Washington has not struck Iran since 1 September. Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced a military campaign against the Houthis, who claimed three operations against Saudi airports, an oil facility and military sites after a fire at an Aramco site near Riyadh; a US carrier group and an amphibious group are heading for the region, which would bring the US to three carriers by the end of October. Rabobank warns that the shuttle system through the strait is fragile; Standard Chartered says flows are far from normal. API stocks are due tonight.

bullets.title: The euro, the yen and the week: French spreads, Ueda today, then the minutes and CPI
bullets.text: The euro touched about $1.116 on Monday, its lowest since May 2025, and is near $1.12 this morning, down 3.4% over a month; the French ten-year yield traded near 4.92–5.0%, the premium over Germany reached about 141bp, the widest since 2012, before narrowing to about 137bp, the government conceded a 5.4% deficit this year against a 5% target, and Prime Minister Sanchez called a snap election in Spain. ING says about 30bp has come out of expected ECB tightening since late September against 13bp for the Fed; UOB expects a pause on 29 October and a final hike in December; Lane said rising long-term rates will slow growth and spill over to inflation. September's euro-area inflation was 3.8%, a three-year high. The dollar index is about 102.1. USD/JPY is 158.1: the BoJ's Ueda speaks at 02:35 ET after the Tokyo close, and sources say the Bank may judge underlying inflation to have reached its 2% goal in the outlook report for its 29–30 October meeting, though the Tankan's corporate-inflation readings moved sideways, which takes pressure off a back-to-back hike. Today: euro-area retail sales at 05:00 ET, the trade balance at 08:30 seen at a $102 billion deficit, Williams at 09:05, Musalem and Bowman at 10:45, Schmid at 13:15 and the three-year auction at 13:00. Wednesday: the ten-year auction at 13:00 and the FOMC minutes at 14:00. Thursday: the ECB's meeting accounts at 07:30, claims at 08:30 seen 200,000, Waller at 04:30, the thirty-year auction at 13:00 and Musalem at 13:40. Friday: Canada's jobs report and Michigan sentiment at 10:00 seen 47.6. CPI is on the 14th.

calendar.note: After the Tokyo close. Sources say the Bank may judge underlying inflation to have reached 2% in its 29–30 October outlook report; the Tankan showed corporate inflation moving sideways. USD/JPY is 158.1 and the ten-year JGB yield about 3.1%.
Seen at a $102 billion deficit after $88.6 billion, which would be the first above $100 billion since March of last year. The week's other data are light before the minutes.

calendar.event: Fed's Williams; Musalem and Bowman 10:45; Schmid 13:15
calendar.note: Williams' 'no need for urgency' on 29 September began the October repricing. With ISM prices at 74.0 and the ten-year at 5.31%, the question is whether any of the four lean the other way.
The first coupon auction since the ten-year touched 5.349%. The last three-year cleared at 4.474%; the two-year is 4.84% now.
The week's test of term premium: the last ten-year cleared at 4.834%, and the benchmark is about 47bp higher. BMO Asset Management calls a thirty-year yield above 6% inevitable this month.
The record of the 12–0 hike. How many of the twelve wanted a faster path, and how the committee discussed the energy shock, with October about 20–22% priced and Logan wanting half a point more.

The accounts of 10 September land after inflation printed 3.8% and French yields neared 5%. Claims seen 200,000 after 197,000; Waller speaks at 04:30 and Musalem at 13:40. PepsiCo reports before the open.

Seen 47.6 after 48.1, the series low; one-year inflation expectations were 4.6%. Canada's jobs report is at 08:30 ET (unemployment seen 6.5%), and Delta reports. The bond market is shut on Monday 12th.

sessionNote: Tuesday opens with Asia and Europe leaning on a Nasdaq record and a ten-year at a 24-year high, which is the same divergence Monday showed: the growth trade is priced on a Fed that has paused, while the long end is priced on supply, energy and term premium. The US session has no scheduled catalyst before 08:30 ET except Ueda's speech at 02:35 ET, then four Fed speakers between 09:05 and 13:15 and the three-year auction at 13:00, which is the first read of demand at these yields. Brent is $100–101 with exports recovering and tankers still being hit; the Qatar-relayed US response is expected today. The real and Brazilian assets hold Monday's move into the runoff on 25 October, and the euro and French spread hold Monday's lows into the 7–8 October auctions. A day to read the auction tail and the two-year, not the headline index.
watchOut: Reading a record Nasdaq as a verdict on the bond market. Monday's index gain came on one stock, Nvidia, a day when the equal-weight S&P 500 fund is down about 3.6% over a month against a 0.7% gain for the cap-weighted index; the ten-year closed near 5.31% on the same day, and the ISM prices line says the inflation argument is intact. Second, Brazil: a 7.7% equity day and a 4% currency day are the largest in years, and the first-round figure is not a result; a runoff in under three weeks means the same assets can move again in either direction. Third, Brent's five-day column: the table still compares December with a day when November was the front month, and Friday's 'Brent rose on the week' headlines have the same roll in them. Fourth, thin Asia: mainland China is shut until 8 October and the Nikkei near 70,700 is trading on the Nasdaq. Size for the three-year auction at 13:00 ET and four Fed speakers, not for the index.

archive.headline: Payrolls 29,000. Yields rose anyway.
archive.summary: September payrolls rose 29,000 against about 90,000 expected with a net 60,000 downward revision, unemployment 4.2% and wages +0.1%; October's Fed hike went to about 22% priced and the Nasdaq touched a record, but the ten-year closed about 3bp higher after Logan said half a point more is needed. The G7 agreed a 100 million barrel stock release, euro-area inflation printed 3.8%, Tokyo core CPI 2.7% and the dollar index reached a 17-month high.

archive.headline: Payrolls 29,000. Yields rose anyway.
archive.summary: Weekend edition. October's Fed hike went from more than 70% priced on Monday to about 25% by Thursday on Williams, a 3.0% core PCE and Jefferson, while the long end set 2002 highs on a 2.2% GDP revision, a 58.8 Chicago PMI and ISM prices paid at 77.9; the ten-year touched 5.344% and closed 5.233%. Brent rose 4.4% on China's fuel-export halt and a third US carrier group, Nike cut its guidance, the euro hit a 16-month low on France's budget and Tokyo core CPI printed 2.7%.

archive.summary: Weekend edition. archive.headline: Core PCE 3.0%. Bonds' worst month since 2022.
archive.summary: Core PCE printed 3.0% against 3.3% after the BEA's annual revision rewrote July, ADP beat at 90,000, final Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% and Chicago PMI jumped to 58.8; October's hike odds slid to 35–40% while the ten-year and thirty-year rose again to close a September in which the ten-year added about 50bp, its worst month since 2022. Micron beat and guided above consensus; the November Brent contract expired at $103.53; the Nikkei rose 3.24%.

archive.headline: October hike back to a coin flip.
archive.summary: Job openings fell to a five-month low, consumer confidence to a 2014 low and Williams said there was 'no need for urgency', taking October's hike from about 70% to about 50% priced; the two-year fell 6bp while the thirty-year touched 5.621%, its highest since 2002. Brent settled 2.6% lower on recovering Saudi exports, Australia's CPI printed 4.0% and the Aussie fell through 70 cents.

archive.headline: The ten-year closed at 5.24%. Nothing else mattered.
archive.summary: The ten-year closed at 5.236%, its highest since 2007, and the S&P 500 fell 0.77% to a ten-session low as Trump's rejection of Iran's Hormuz offer put Brent back above $107; Cook and Barkin talked rates higher, gold fell 3% to a seven-week low, and the RBA hiked to 4.60% overnight. The November Brent roll and Washington's reply to Tehran via Qatar were the day's traps.

archive.headline: Trump said no. Oil is back above $107.
archive.summary: Trump rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz offer over the weekend and Brent recovered Friday's fall before New York opened; gold fell to its lowest since early August, the Kospi lost 2.5% and the dollar hit a two-month high. The front end eased with October's hike odds while the long end kept rising, into a week of PCE, ISM and payrolls.
